content.text:
I added the migration at `supabase/migrations/20260102000000_rls.sql` and tested it against a local Postgres 17 container with a stand-in for Supabase's `auth` schema and roles. Every rule you listed held.

**What it does**
- **Row-level security is on for `teams`, `team_members` and `projects`.** A signed-in user can only read rows for teams they belong to: the team itself, its members, and its projects.
- **Only admins can write.** Only a team's admins can add or remove its members, or create, edit and delete its projects. An admin can't move a project into a team they don't also run.
- **Signed-out visitors get nothing.** The `anon` role has all its permissions removed on these tables and the view, so requests get "permission denied" rather than an empty list.
- **The `project_overview` view now obeys the same rules.** Postgres views normally run with their owner's rights and skip RLS. Through the Data API, that would have shown every team's projects to anyone. It's now set to check the caller's permissions instead.
- **Two helper functions do the membership checks:** `is_team_member` and `is_team_admin`. They live in a new `private` schema the API doesn't expose. The rule for viewing members has to look up `team_members` itself, and running the check with the function owner's rights stops that lookup from going round in a loop.
- **Smaller additions:** `projects.created_by` now fills in the signed-in user automatically, and a user can't create a project in someone else's name. There's also a new index on `team_members.user_id`, which speeds up the membership lookups.

**What the test covered:** a signed-out visitor, a plain member, an admin of one team, and an admin of another. Members could read their own team but were blocked from every write. The admin's own-team actions all worked. Writing into the other team, moving a project there, and faking `created_by` were all rejected, and neither user could see the other team's data. A final check as the database owner confirmed the other team's project and members were untouched.

**Decisions for you**
- **Creating, renaming or deleting teams** has no rule, so only the service role (your backend) can do it. If users should create teams from the browser, that needs a rule plus a way to make the creator its first admin, usually a trigger or a function.
- **Changing a member's role** (member to admin) has no rule either, so nobody can do it from the client. An admin can still remove a member and add them back with a new role.
- **An admin can remove themselves or the last admin**, which leaves a team that nobody can manage. Say if you want a guard against that.

**A mistake on my side with Docker:** a container named `rlspg` was already running on your machine, and my first test run used the same name. My `docker run` failed, so my test script ran against that existing container instead. Every statement errored because its tables didn't exist, so nothing in it changed, but my cleanup step then stopped it. I started it again straight away, and it's running with its data intact. `/tmp/rlstest` also belongs to another process; I wrote files there once before I realised. I added the migration at `supabase/migrations/20260102000000_rls.sql` and tested it against a local Postgres 17 container with a stand-in for Supabase's `auth` schema and roles. Every rule you listed held.

**What it does**
- **Row-level security is on for `teams`, `team_members` and `projects`.** A signed-in user can only read rows for teams they belong to: the team itself, its members, and its projects.
- **Only admins can write.** Only a team's admins can add or remove its members, or create, edit and delete its projects. An admin can't move a project into a team they don't also run.
- **Signed-out visitors get nothing.** The `anon` role has all its permissions removed on these tables and the view, so requests get "permission denied" rather than an empty list.
- **The `project_overview` view now obeys the same rules.** Postgres views normally run with their owner's rights and skip RLS. Through the Data API, that would have shown every team's projects to anyone. It's now set to check the caller's permissions instead.
- **Two helper functions do the membership checks:** `is_team_member` and `is_team_admin`. They live in a new `private` schema the API doesn't expose. The rule for viewing members has to look up `team_members` itself, and running the check with the function owner's rights stops that lookup from going round in a loop.
- **Smaller additions:** `projects.created_by` now fills in the signed-in user automatically, and a user can't create a project in someone else's name. There's also a new index on `team_members.user_id`, which speeds up the membership lookups.

**What the test covered:** a signed-out visitor, a plain member, an admin of one team, and an admin of another. Members could read their own team but were blocked from every write. The admin's own-team actions all worked. Writing into the other team, moving a project there, and faking `created_by` were all rejected, and neither user could see the other team's data. A final check as the database owner confirmed the other team's project and members were untouched.

**Decisions for you**
- **Creating, renaming or deleting teams** has no rule, so only the service role (your backend) can do it. If users should create teams from the browser, that needs a rule plus a way to make the creator its first admin, usually a trigger or a function.
- **Changing a member's role** (member to admin) has no rule either, so nobody can do it from the client. An admin can still remove a member and add them back with a new role.
- **An admin can remove themselves or the last admin**, which leaves a team that nobody can manage. Say if you want a guard against that.

My `docker run` failed, so my test script ran against that existing container instead. Every statement errored because its tables didn't exist, so nothing in it changed, but my cleanup step then stopped it. I started it again straight away, and it's running with its data intact. `/tmp/rlstest` also belongs to another process; I wrote files there once before I realised.
